title: Kratos Defense Reports Record Backlog as Drone Sales Slide
subtitle: Hypersonics and propulsion carry the quarterly print while the flagship unmanned division contracts
summary: Kratos delivered double-digit revenue growth and expanded its record order backlog on surging demand for rocket systems and specialized electronics. However, declining sales in its flagship unmanned drone unit and widening cash burns show the company is operating as a component supplier rather than an autonomous platform winner.

bodyHtml:
If you bought Kratos for the killer robot drones, you bought a plumbing contractor with rocket fuel. Investors spent the year treating the defense outfit as the pure-play champion of cheap, AI-enabled combat aircraft swarming contested skies. Then the third-quarter report arrived.

Consolidated revenue surged nearly 36% to $471.8 million, but the celebrated drone division shrank 14%.

Kratos makes the unglamorous physical skeleton of modern war. The San Diego contractor builds subscale jet-powered target drones, hypersonic rocket boosters, micro-turbojet engines, and microwave electronics that steer missile radar and satellite networks. It sells primarily to the Pentagon, NASA, and allied militaries through slow, formal budget cycles.

Think of modern autonomous warfare like consumer electronics: Silicon Valley startups design the flashy software brains, but Kratos welds the aluminum chassis, wires the battery pack, and casts the engine blades.

That role matters because military artificial intelligence cannot fight without physical bodies. Strategists call this attritable mass—machines cheap enough to lose in combat without causing a fiscal crisis. Kratos builds the airframe, installs the propulsion, and operates the live-fire test ranges where the tech proves itself.

It is an indispensable shovel-seller for the autonomous era. Yet that division of labor assigns Kratos the thin operating margins and heavy working capital of an industrial metal-bender, not the high-margin software economics Wall Street originally priced in.

The quarterly numbers laid that identity crisis bare. Revenue in the core government solutions unit jumped over 52% to $397.2 million, powered by defense rocket systems more than doubling their shipments. That side of the house booked two and a half dollars of new work for every dollar out the door.

Meanwhile, the Unmanned Systems segment slipped to $74.6 million, fell into an operating loss, and booked only 80 cents of work for every dollar delivered. The company-wide backlog expanded, but the drone backlog went backwards.

The marquee prestige has migrated as well. The Air Force awarded its defining Collaborative Combat Aircraft Increment 1 contracts to rivals Anduril and General Atomics, leaving Kratos on the outside of the military's top autonomous fighter program. To stay in that fight, Kratos is now playing subcontractor, supplying airframes for a Marine Corps project led by Northrop and developing a small turbofan engine with GE Aerospace.

Its Valkyrie drone completed its first European flight with Airbus mission software in the autumn, proving export demand is real, but the prime domestic trophies belong to someone else.

The short seller's argument writes itself in that shortfall. The drone premium was the stock's entire valuation thesis, and that business is actively losing altitude while burning cash. Full-year operating cash flow guidance was cut from tens of millions down to roughly flat, while free cash flow burn widened past $110 million.

Non-cash compensation, amortization, and internal research wiped out operating gains to produce a small net loss. Kratos is breaking ground on new radar facilities and hypersonics arc-jet complexes in Indiana, but bankrolling factory floors for orders tethered to a divided Congress trapped under a continuing resolution is precarious. If free cash flow remains negative into late 2027 once federal budgets finally settle, this ambitious buildout is simply an expensive cash furnace.

The counterweight is that the rest of the arsenal is selling faster than factories can assemble it. Consolidated backlog hit a record $2.65 billion, backed by a bidding pipeline worth $15.5 billion. Kratos is building an entrenched tollbooth in hypersonics testing, anticipating roughly $700 million in hypersonic revenue next year alone.

Furthermore, roughly $1.4 billion in balance-sheet cash provides real breathing room against Washington gridlock, which explains why sell-side analysts have slashed their price targets without abandoning their buy recommendations.

For the equity to mount a sustained recovery, two specific conditions must fall into place. First, federal lawmakers must pass an official defense appropriation by spring to release the frozen program funding management is counting on. Second, that record backlog must prove it can convert into positive free cash flow.

What we are watching is the late February full-year report, when leadership reveals its initial cash forecasts alongside progress on the Air Force engine downselect scheduled for mid-2027. If cash begins flowing back to shareholders, the market can finally price the company for the industrial engine it actually is.

A vital supplier holding a record backlog does not need to masquerade as a software platform to win.
